content: Nordic walking (NW) has been suggested as a potential intervention to enhance rehabilitation outcomes in individuals with Parkinson’s disease (PD). The primary objective of this systematic review was to evaluate the existing evidence on the effects of NW in rehabilitation programs for PD patients and to propose a standardized design for future research to improve consistency across studies. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across five established databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane) to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published in English up to February 2017. The review adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, and the methodological quality of each study was assessed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro) scale. Out of 66 studies initially retrieved, six RCTs involving 221 participants were included in the qualitative synthesis. These studies demonstrated that NW is a feasible and potentially effective intervention for improving functional and clinical outcomes in individuals with PD. However, when NW was compared to other exercise-based interventions, such as treadmill training, free walking, standardized whole-body movement programs (e.g., Lee Silverman Voice Treatment BIG training), or home-based exercise programs, the findings were inconsistent. The high heterogeneity and methodological discrepancies among the studies precluded definitive conclusions regarding the comparative effectiveness of NW versus other interventions. Further research with standardized designs is necessary to determine whether NW can be integrated into conventional rehabilitation programs for PD patients. Tai Chi has also been investigated as a therapeutic exercise for improving physical function and well-being in individuals with PD. Current medical treatments for PD are primarily palliative, but research suggests that Tai Chi may enhance balance and certain aspects of well-being. A systematic review of the literature, including 11 studies (7 RCTs and 4 quasi-experimental studies) with 548 participants (mean age 68 years, 50% women), revealed that Tai Chi participants exhibited better balance and improvements in well-being, although the results were mixed. The review highlighted the need for more rigorous study designs, larger sample sizes, adequate Tai Chi exercise doses, and carefully selected outcome measures to assess both the mechanisms and effects of Tai Chi before widespread recommendations can be made. Dance-based interventions have also been explored for their potential to improve functional mobility, motor symptoms, and quality of life (QoL) in PD patients. A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs compared the effects of dance classes to other interventions or no intervention. Five RCTs involving 159 participants demonstrated that dance significantly improved motor symptoms (as measured by the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale III) and reduced Timed Up and Go (TUG) test times compared to other exercise types. Dance also showed significant improvements in motor scores compared to no intervention. These findings suggest that dance can enhance motor parameters and functional mobility in PD patients. However, the review emphasized the need for further research to determine the optimal intensity, frequency, duration of dance interventions, and the most beneficial music. Another systematic review focused on the effects of dance on gait, cognition, and dual-tasking in PD patients. This review critically appraised and synthesized evidence from 12 studies with sufficient common assessment items for meta-analysis. Dance interventions were associated with significant improvements in gait speed, TUG test performance, freezing of gait, and six-minute walk test times compared to controls. Global cognition (assessed with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment) and cognitive dual-tasking (measured using dual-task TUG) also improved in dance groups. However, the evidence was limited regarding the most effective intensity, frequency, and duration of dance interventions or the most beneficial music. The findings must be interpreted cautiously due to the lack of RCTs and the moderate-to-high risk of bias in the included studies. Nonetheless, dance appears to have the potential to ameliorate PD symptoms, particularly gait, global cognition, and cognitive dual-tasking. Finally, a systematic review examined the effects of different exercise modes (aerobic, resistance, and coordination training) on domain-specific cognitive function in PD patients. The review included 11 RCTs with 508 participants (mean age 68 years) and disease severity ranging from stages 1 to 4 on the Hoehn & Yahr scale. All exercise modes were associated with improved cognitive function, with aerobic exercise showing a tendency to best improve memory. However, no clear effect of exercise mode was identified. The review highlighted the need for further research to establish the most effective exercise interventions for cognitive improvement in PD patients.
